entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Well known and closely watched by the public and the media, so that what you do is noticed and discussed.
entries.usage: Used about celebrities, athletes, business leaders and their families, usually after *be*, *live*, *stay* or *grow up*. It is neutral and often stresses the pressure and the lack of privacy that come with fame. The common opposite is *out of the public eye*: *She has stayed out of the public eye since she retired.*
entries.pattern: be / live / grow up in the public eye; stay out of the public eye
examples: Growing up **in the public eye** wasn't easy for the actor's kids; photographers followed them to school.
After twenty years **in the public eye**, the news anchor moved to a quiet farm in Vermont.
When you run a company that size, you're **in the public eye** whether you like it or not.

drill.sentence: Being a pro quarterback means living {{in the public eye}}; even what you order at a restaurant ends up online.
drill.hint: watched by everyone, including the media (not *in the spotlight*)

entries.related: *in the spotlight* — receiving a lot of attention, often for a shorter time; *a public figure* — a person who is in the public eye; *keep a low profile* — avoid attention.

entries.term: one step forward, two steps back
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Describes a situation in which each bit of progress is followed by a bigger setback, so that overall things go nowhere or get worse.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and journalism about frustrating projects, reforms, diets or recovery from an illness. It often stands alone as a comment: *It's one step forward, two steps back.* The reverse, *two steps forward, one step back*, is more hopeful: real progress with small setbacks.
examples: My diet is **one step forward, two steps back**: I eat well all week and then undo it all on Saturday.
Every update fixes one bug and creates two new ones; it's **one step forward, two steps back** with this app.
Physical therapy after his knee surgery felt like **one step forward, two steps back**, because every good week ended with new swelling.

drill.sentence: We finally got the kitchen painted, and then a pipe burst and ruined the floor. It's {{one step forward, two steps back}} with this house.
drill.hint: every gain followed by a bigger loss (the pessimistic version)

entries.related: *two steps forward, one step back* — progress despite small setbacks; *back to square one* — back at the very start; *spin your wheels* — work hard without making progress.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A very short distance, close enough to walk to easily.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, travel writing and real estate ads, usually as *a stone's throw from* or *within a stone's throw of* a place. It is friendly and positive and usually stresses convenience. Without a place, people add *away*: *The beach is just a stone's throw away.*
entries.pattern: (just) a stone's throw from / within a stone's throw of + place
examples: We rented a cabin just **a stone's throw** from the lake, so the kids could swim every morning.
The new apartments are **a stone's throw** from the subway, which explains the rent.
My wife and I lived within **a stone's throw** of each other for years before we ever met.

drill.sentence: Our hotel was {{a stone's throw}} from the Colosseum, so we walked over before the crowds arrived.
drill.hint: a very short distance (a rock image; not *a short walk*)

entries.related: *a hop, skip and a jump* — same, more playful; *around the corner* — very near, often in a town; *within walking distance* — plain and neutral.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A subject that people disagree about and keep arguing over, often for a long time.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal; common in journalism, business and stories about family or neighbors. Typical patterns are *a (major) bone of contention between A and B* and *remain a bone of contention*. It names the topic of the dispute, not the argument itself.
entries.pattern: a bone of contention (between A and B)
examples: Who gets the car on weekends has become **a bone of contention** between my two teenagers.
Parking has long been **a bone of contention** between the restaurant and its neighbors.
Salary wasn't the problem in the negotiations; the real **bone of contention** was working from home.

drill.sentence: The thermostat is a constant {{bone of contention}} in our office: half of us are freezing and the other half are too hot.
drill.hint: topic people keep fighting over (a dog image; not *point of …*)

entries.related: *a point of contention* — same, more formal and less vivid; *a sore point* — a topic that upsets someone; *a sticking point* — an issue that blocks an agreement.
entries.origin: From the image of two dogs fighting over a single bone.

entries.term: take the words right out of someone's mouth
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say exactly what another person was about to say or was thinking.
entries.usage: A friendly, casual reply that shows strong agreement: *You took the words right out of my mouth!* It is almost always in the past tense with *my mouth*. *Right* is often left out: *You took the words out of my mouth.*
entries.pattern: You took the words (right) out of my mouth.
examples: When my sister said we should skip the party, she **took the words right out of my mouth**.
"This movie is way too long." "You **took the words right out of my mouth**."
I was about to raise the same concern about the budget, but Priya **took the words right out of my mouth**.

drill.sentence: "Honestly, let's just order takeout tonight." "Yes! You {{took the words right out of my mouth}}."
drill.hint: said exactly what I was about to say (not *read my mind*)

entries.related: *read someone's mind* — know what they are thinking; *great minds think alike* — a joking reply when two people have the same idea; *my thoughts exactly* — plainer agreement.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly become very angry, usually more than the situation deserves.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, often as criticism of someone's temper: *He flies off the handle over nothing.* It describes a sudden loss of control, not long-lasting anger. Typical partners are *at* + person, *over* + cause, and *every time*.
entries.pattern: fly off the handle (at someone / over something)
examples: My dad used to **fly off the handle** whenever someone left the lights on.
I'm sorry I **flew off the handle** at you yesterday; I was stressed about money.
A driver **flew off the handle** when I took the parking spot he'd been waiting for.

drill.sentence: Don't tell Greg about the scratch on his car yet; he tends to {{fly off the handle}} over little things.
drill.hint: suddenly get very angry (an image of an ax head; not *blow up*)

entries.related: *lose your temper* — neutral; *blow up* — similar, informal; *hit the roof* — get very angry, often at news.
entries.origin: An American phrase from the early 1800s, based on the image of an ax head flying off a loose handle.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who behaves as if they know everything and ignores what other people know or think.
entries.usage: Informal and clearly negative; a common insult in families, schools and offices. People often say *I don't want to sound like a know-it-all, but …* before correcting someone. It also works before a noun: *his know-it-all attitude*; British English also has *know-all*.
examples: Nobody wants to play trivia with Jake anymore; he's such **a know-it-all**.
I don't want to sound like **a know-it-all**, but that restaurant closed two years ago.
Her **know-it-all** tone in meetings annoys even the people who agree with her.

drill.sentence: My brother-in-law is {{a know-it-all}}; at Thanksgiving dinner he explained my own job to me.
drill.hint: someone who acts as if he has every answer (not *smart aleck*)

entries.related: *smart aleck* — someone who makes clever, rude remarks; *wise guy* — similar, American; *show-off* — someone who wants to impress others.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of a relationship, especially a marriage: having serious problems and likely to end soon.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation and celebrity news: *Their marriage is on the rocks.* It is used mostly about couples, sometimes about businesses or deals. Don't confuse it with the bar meaning: a drink *on the rocks* is served over ice.
examples: Their marriage was **on the rocks** long before he moved out.
Rumors that the couple's relationship is **on the rocks** have been all over the gossip sites this week.
After two bad years, the family business was **on the rocks**, and the bank wanted its money back.

drill.sentence: They seemed so happy at the wedding, but by their second anniversary the marriage was already {{on the rocks}}.
drill.hint: in serious trouble and close to ending (a shipwreck image; not *falling apart*)

entries.related: *on the ropes* — close to defeat; *in trouble* — plainer; *going through a rough patch* — having a difficult period that may pass.
entries.origin: From ships that hit rocks and break apart.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To earn the money that a family needs to live on, especially as the main earner.
entries.usage: Informal and a little humorous; mostly used when talking about who earns the main income in a household. It often appears in contrast with staying home or doing the housework. The form is fixed, always with *the bacon*.
examples: In our house, my wife **brings home the bacon** and I do most of the cooking.
With three kids and a mortgage, he worked two jobs just to **bring home the bacon**.
Between his day job and weekend gigs with his band, Marco **brings home the bacon** for a family of six.

drill.sentence: After Dad lost his job, Mom went back to nursing full-time and {{brought home the bacon}} for the next ten years.
drill.hint: earned the family's income (a breakfast-meat image; not *paid the bills*)

entries.related: *be the breadwinner* — earn the main income, neutral; *put food on the table* — earn enough to feed a family; *make ends meet* — just manage to pay for basic needs.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: It is very important to act quickly, because a delay could cause serious problems.
entries.usage: Formal and serious; common in business emails, legal texts, medicine and news about emergencies. It is usually a full clause: *Time is of the essence, so please reply by Friday.* In a contract, a *time is of the essence* clause means the deadlines are strict and missing one is a breach.
examples: With a stroke, **time is of the essence**: every minute without treatment can cause lasting damage.
**Time is of the essence**, so please sign and return the documents by Friday.
If you want tickets to the reunion tour, **time is of the essence**; they'll be gone in minutes.

drill.sentence: The house next door just went on the market and several buyers are interested, so {{time is of the essence}} if you want to make an offer.
drill.hint: acting fast is critical (a formal phrase; not *every minute counts*)

entries.related: *every minute counts* — same idea, less formal; *there's no time to lose* — urgent, spoken; *ASAP* — as soon as possible, informal in emails.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: From being very poor to being very rich, usually through your own work or talent.
entries.usage: Used in news, biographies and conversation about inspiring life stories. It often appears as *go from rags to riches* or as the noun phrase *a rags-to-riches story*, hyphenated before a noun. The reverse, *from riches to rags*, describes losing everything.
entries.pattern: go from rags to riches; a rags-to-riches story
examples: The chain's founder went **from rags to riches**, starting with one taco truck and ending up with forty restaurants.
It's a classic **rags-to-riches** story: a kid from a poor neighborhood becomes an NBA star.
The singer often talks about her journey **from rags to riches**, from a homeless shelter to sold-out stadiums.

drill.sentence: The documentary follows a farm boy who went {{from rags to riches}} by building one of the country's biggest trucking companies.
drill.hint: from poverty to great wealth (a clothing image)

entries.related: *self-made* — rich or successful through your own effort; *a Cinderella story* — an unknown person who suddenly succeeds; *strike it rich* — become rich suddenly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The best people or things in a group, chosen from many.
entries.usage: Positive and common when talking about students, athletes, job candidates or products. It is usually *the cream of the crop*, with *the*, and it stresses that these were selected from a large number. In formal writing it can sound like a cliché.
examples: The academy only accepts **the cream of the crop**, so getting in is a big deal.
Of all the apartments we saw, this one is definitely **the cream of the crop**.
The scholarship goes to **the cream of the crop**: about twenty students out of five thousand applicants.

drill.sentence: Navy SEAL candidates are already {{the cream of the crop}}, yet most of them still fail the training.
drill.hint: the very best of a group (a dairy image; not *the best of the best*)

entries.related: *the best of the best* — same, more emphatic; *top-notch* — excellent, an adjective; *the pick of the litter* — the best one of a group, informal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation, place or person so dangerous or badly organized that an accident or a problem is almost certain.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, usually as a warning or a complaint about roads, equipment, buildings or careless people. It is also said after an accident, to say it was predictable. *A disaster waiting to happen* means the same and sounds stronger.
examples: That intersection with no traffic light is **an accident waiting to happen**.
Everyone knew the old bridge was **an accident waiting to happen**, but the county kept postponing repairs.
Putting a trampoline right next to the pool seemed like **an accident waiting to happen**, so we moved it.

drill.sentence: With loose wires hanging from the ceiling and boxes blocking the exits, that warehouse is {{an accident waiting to happen}}.
drill.hint: a place where harm is almost certain (not *a disaster …* or *a death trap*)

entries.related: *a disaster waiting to happen* — same, stronger; *a death trap* — a very dangerous place or vehicle; *a ticking time bomb* — a problem that will explode later.

entries.term: fly by the seat of your pants
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something without a plan or proper preparation, relying on instinct and improvising as you go.
entries.usage: Informal; it can sound admiring or self-mocking, but it usually admits a lack of preparation. It is often in the progressive: *We're flying by the seat of our pants.* *Seat-of-the-pants* also works as an adjective: *a seat-of-the-pants operation*.
examples: We had no idea how to run a restaurant; for the first year we were **flying by the seat of our pants**.
I didn't have time to prepare for the interview, so I just **flew by the seat of my pants**.
Most new parents **fly by the seat of their pants** for the first few months.

drill.sentence: Our tour guide quit on the second day, so we {{flew by the seat of our pants}} for the rest of the trip through Peru.
drill.hint: improvised without a plan (an early-pilot image; not *winged it*)

entries.related: *wing it* — do something without preparation; *play it by ear* — decide as things develop; *make it up as you go along* — improvise.
entries.origin: From early aviation, when pilots flew without instruments and judged the plane's movement by feel.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A short period when an ordinary person is famous, often by chance, before people forget them.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and media commentary, often slightly mocking or ironic. Typical verbs are *have*, *get* and *enjoy*, usually with a possessive: *She had her fifteen minutes of fame.* It suggests the fame was accidental and won't last.
examples: A video of his dog skateboarding went viral, and he got his **fifteen minutes of fame**.
She had her **fifteen minutes of fame** as a game show contestant in the nineties.
Reality TV gives a lot of people **fifteen minutes of fame** and very little else.

drill.sentence: After the local news interviewed him about the giant pumpkin he grew, my uncle enjoyed his {{fifteen minutes of fame}}.
drill.hint: brief moment of celebrity (an artist's famous number)

entries.related: *a flash in the pan* — a success that does not last; *a one-hit wonder* — an artist known for only one hit; *in the spotlight* — receiving public attention.
entries.origin: From Andy Warhol's 1968 remark that in the future everyone will be world-famous for fifteen minutes.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To become gradually worse in quality, health or condition.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and neutral writing about restaurants, neighborhoods, health, relationships and careers. Typical patterns are *go downhill fast* and *has gone downhill since …*. It describes a decline over time, not one sudden event.
entries.pattern: go downhill (fast); has gone downhill since …
examples: This pizza place has really **gone downhill** since the new owners took over.
My grandfather's health **went downhill** quickly after his fall last winter.
The party started well, but it **went downhill** fast once the karaoke machine came out.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood {{went downhill}} after the factory closed and half the stores on Main Street were boarded up.
drill.hint: got steadily worse (a slope image; not *declined* or *… south*)

entries.related: *go to pot* — become ruined through neglect, informal; *take a turn for the worse* — suddenly get worse; *go from bad to worse* — get even worse.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Far from the places that tourists usually visit, so quiet and not well known.
entries.usage: Common in travel talk and writing, and usually positive: it suggests a place is authentic and uncrowded. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *an off-the-beaten-path café*. British English prefers *off the beaten track*, which Americans also use.
examples: We skipped the big resorts and found a little fishing village **off the beaten path**.
The guidebook focuses on restaurants **off the beaten path**, where locals actually eat.
Her favorite ski area is a bit **off the beaten path**, so there are never any lines.

drill.sentence: If you want to avoid the crowds in Italy, try some towns {{off the beaten path}} instead of Venice and Florence.
drill.hint: away from the usual tourist routes (the American form, not *… track*)

entries.related: *off the beaten track* — same, more common in British English; *in the middle of nowhere* — very remote, often negative; *a hidden gem* — a good place that few people know.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To show something very clearly without anyone needing to say it in words.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism. The subject is usually an action, a look, a silence or a fact, and *about* often follows: *It speaks volumes about her character.* It can be positive or negative.
entries.pattern: something speaks volumes (about someone / something)
examples: She said nothing when I asked about her new boss, but the look on her face **spoke volumes**.
The fact that half the staff quit in one year **speaks volumes** about the management.
He drove four hours in a snowstorm to help us move; that **speaks volumes**.

drill.sentence: Nobody from the band showed up at the award ceremony, and their absence {{spoke volumes}}.
drill.hint: communicated a lot without words (a book image; not *said it all*)

entries.related: *say it all* — show everything that needs to be known; *tell you everything you need to know* — plainer; *actions speak louder than words* — what you do matters more than what you say.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very upset, angry or offended, especially about something that is not important.
entries.usage: Informal American English, often as advice in the negative: *Don't get bent out of shape over it.* It suggests the reaction is too strong for the cause. The usual verb is *get*, and the cause follows *over* or *about*.
entries.pattern: get (all) bent out of shape over / about something
examples: My roommate got all **bent out of shape** because I ate one of his yogurts.
Some fans got **bent out of shape** over the new jersey design, but it sold out anyway.
I don't know why he's so **bent out of shape**; I only said the steak was a little dry.

drill.sentence: Relax, it's only a tiny scratch on the bumper. There's no need to get {{bent out of shape}} over it.
drill.hint: overly upset about something minor — a twisted-metal image (not *worked up*)

entries.related: *worked up* — upset or excited, neutral; *make a big deal out of something* — treat it as more important than it is; *take offense* — feel insulted.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who hides nothing, so their thoughts, feelings and life are easy to know.
entries.usage: Usually positive or neutral: *I'm an open book* means you are happy to answer any question. It can also mean someone cannot hide their feelings: *His face is an open book.* The opposite, *a closed book*, is a person who is hard to understand.
examples: Ask me anything you want; I'm **an open book**.
My son is **an open book**: when something's wrong at school, I know before he says a word.
Unlike her quiet sister, Lena is **an open book** and tells everyone about her dating life.

drill.sentence: You'll never win at poker, Jen. Your face is {{an open book}}.
drill.hint: something anyone can read easily (a reading image)

entries.related: *wear your heart on your sleeve* — show your feelings openly; *a closed book* — the opposite; *a poker face* — a face that shows no feelings.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A perfect combination of two people or two things that suit each other extremely well.
entries.usage: Used about couples, business partners and combinations of food, styles or ideas, often with warmth or humor: *Peanut butter and chocolate are a match made in heaven.* The form is fixed. *A match made in hell* is a joke about a terrible pairing.
examples: My parents have been married forty years; they're **a match made in heaven**.
The bakery opened a coffee bar next door, and the two businesses turned out to be **a match made in heaven**.
A shy writer and a loud producer didn't sound like **a match made in heaven**, but their show ran for ten years.

drill.sentence: Mike loves to cook and Sara loves to eat; honestly, they're {{a match made in heaven}}.
drill.hint: a perfect pairing — a noun phrase with a divine image

entries.related: *made for each other* — perfectly suited, about couples; *a perfect fit* — plainer; *go together like …* — combine well, often about food.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To sell very quickly and in large numbers.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, retail and business news. The subject is the product, and the verb is usually in the progressive or the past: *The new phones are selling like hotcakes.* *Hotcakes* is an American word for pancakes; British writers often spell it *hot cakes*.
examples: The kids' lemonade **sold like hotcakes** during the heat wave.
Her cookbook **sold like hotcakes** after she appeared on a morning talk show.
The new phone is **selling like hotcakes**, and most stores ran out on the first day.

drill.sentence: Those dinosaur costumes are {{selling like hotcakes}}, so if you want one for your daughter, buy it today.
drill.hint: being bought very fast (a breakfast-food image; not *flying off the shelves*)

entries.related: *fly off the shelves* — sell very fast; *a best seller* — a product that sells very well; *sell out* — sell every item available.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something quickly or a lot because you started late or missed chances to do it earlier.
entries.usage: Very common and usually positive and energetic, for example after an illness, a separation or a late start. The form is fixed: *lost time*, with no article. It often describes people enjoying something with extra intensity: *Now he's making up for lost time.*
examples: My dad didn't travel at all until he retired, so now he's **making up for lost time**.
After two years apart, the brothers spent the whole summer together, **making up for lost time**.
We started the project a month late, so we're working weekends to **make up for lost time**.

drill.sentence: She didn't learn to swim until she was forty, but she's {{making up for lost time}} with three swims a week.
drill.hint: doing a lot to compensate for her late start (not *catching up* or *playing catch-up*)

entries.related: *catch up* — reach the level of others; *play catch-up* — try to reach others after falling behind; *better late than never* — doing it late is better than not doing it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly have new energy to continue after you have been feeling tired.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work and social life: *By midnight I'd gotten a second wind.* *Get*, *catch* and *find* are all used. It can also describe a project or a career that becomes active again, but the energy sense is the basic one.
entries.pattern: get / catch / find a second wind
examples: I was exhausted at mile twenty, but then I **got a second wind** and finished strong.
We were ready to leave the party at eleven, but after some coffee we **got a second wind** and danced until two.
Around four in the afternoon, most of the office slows down, but Dana always seems to **get a second wind**.

drill.sentence: The kids looked half asleep in the car, but the moment we got to the beach they {{got a second wind}} and ran straight into the water.
drill.hint: suddenly found new energy (a breathing image; not *perked up*)

entries.related: *perk up* — become more lively; *recharge your batteries* — rest to get energy back; *run out of steam* — the opposite, lose energy.
entries.origin: From running: after the first tiredness, breathing gets easier and a runner can keep going.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of the highest quality; excellent.
entries.usage: Informal to neutral and very common in reviews, ads and conversation: *top-notch service*, *The food was top-notch.* It is written with a hyphen. It sounds warm and enthusiastic but is still fine in a work email.
examples: The hotel wasn't fancy, but the service was **top-notch**.
She hired a **top-notch** lawyer, and the case was dropped within a month.
The hospital has **top-notch** heart surgeons, so patients fly in from all over the country.

drill.sentence: We paid a lot for the kitchen remodel, but the workmanship is {{top-notch}}; every cabinet fits perfectly.
drill.hint: of the very best quality — a hyphenated informal word (not *first-rate* or *first-class*)

entries.related: *first-rate* — excellent, slightly more formal; *first-class* — of the best quality; *second-rate* — the opposite, mediocre.

entries.term: out of the frying pan into the fire
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: From a bad situation into one that is even worse, often because of an attempt to escape the first one.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism as a comment on a decision that made things worse: *Talk about out of the frying pan into the fire.* It often follows *go* or *jump*. The version with *and* is just as common: *out of the frying pan and into the fire*.
examples: He quit a job he hated for one with an even worse boss; talk about **out of the frying pan into the fire**.
Moving from my parents' house into an apartment with three messy roommates was **out of the frying pan and into the fire**.
The chain sold its best stores to pay off its debts, and then sales collapsed; it had jumped **out of the frying pan into the fire**.

drill.sentence: I moved out to get away from my noisy roommate, and now my new apartment is right above a nightclub — {{out of the frying pan into the fire}}.
drill.hint: from a bad situation to a worse one (a kitchen image; not *from bad to worse*)

entries.related: *go from bad to worse* — get even worse, without the idea of escaping; *between a rock and a hard place* — facing two bad choices.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Likely to happen in the future.
entries.usage: Informal American English, very often negative: *It just wasn't in the cards.* It is used about plans, relationships and events, and can suggest fate. British English says *on the cards*.
examples: We wanted a big wedding, but with our budget it just wasn't **in the cards**.
A trip to Japan might be **in the cards** for next summer if airfares drop.
With half the team injured, a return to the playoffs isn't **in the cards** this season.

drill.sentence: I'd love to have a third kid, but with our tiny apartment, it's probably not {{in the cards}}.
drill.hint: likely in the future (a fortune-teller image; the American form)

entries.related: *on the cards* — the British form; *on the horizon* — coming soon; *a long shot* — something with little chance of success.
entries.origin: From fortune-telling, in which cards are read to predict the future.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Exactly level or very close in a race or competition, so that either side could still win.
entries.usage: Common in sports commentary, polls and business news about rivals. It usually follows *be* or *run*: *The two teams are neck and neck.* Before a noun it is hyphenated: *a neck-and-neck race*.
examples: With one lap to go, the two runners were **neck and neck**.
The two pizza chains have been running **neck and neck** for the top spot in town for years.
My sister and I were **neck and neck** in our fantasy football league until the very last week.

drill.sentence: Going into the final hole, Garcia and Kim were {{neck and neck}}, so the whole crowd gathered around the green.
drill.hint: exactly level in the competition (a horse-racing image; not *tied* or *even*)

entries.related: *tied* — with exactly the same score; *a close call* — something that almost went the other way; *too close to call* — impossible to predict, often about elections.
entries.origin: From horse racing, where two horses running level have their necks side by side.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Small, careful steps or actions toward a larger goal, especially when you are starting something difficult.
entries.usage: Informal and encouraging; common in conversation, coaching and therapy talk, and *Baby steps!* alone is a common reply to small progress. Typical patterns are *take baby steps* and *in baby steps*. In news it can sound critical: *baby steps* toward a solution may mean too little progress.
entries.pattern: take baby steps (toward something)
examples: I'm not running marathons yet, but I walked two miles today. **Baby steps**.
The company is taking **baby steps** toward a four-day week, starting with Fridays off in July.
If you're new to cooking, start with **baby steps**: eggs first, then pasta, then a simple soup.

drill.sentence: Don't try to clean out the whole garage this weekend. Take {{baby steps}}: one shelf at a time.
drill.hint: small, gradual moves (an infant image)

entries.related: *one step at a time* — slowly and carefully; *a small win* — a minor success; *go all in* — the opposite, commit fully at once.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go straight and quickly toward something or someone, usually because you want it.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation and storytelling, often humorous: *The kids made a beeline for the candy.* It is usually followed by *for*, sometimes by *to*, and then a place, thing or person. It describes physical movement, not a decision.
entries.pattern: make a beeline for / to + place, thing, person
examples: As soon as we walked into the party, my son **made a beeline for** the dessert table.
When the doors opened at six, shoppers **made a beeline for** the discounted TVs.
She spotted her old college roommate across the airport and **made a beeline for** her.

drill.sentence: The moment I got off the plane, I {{made a beeline for}} the nearest coffee shop.
drill.hint: went directly and quickly to (an insect image; not *headed straight for*)

entries.related: *head straight for* — go directly to, plainer; *rush over to* — go quickly; *as the crow flies* — in a straight line, about distance.
entries.origin: From the belief that bees fly back to their hive in a straight line.

entries.term: two sides of the same coin
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Two things that seem different or even opposite but are closely connected, so that one comes with the other.
entries.usage: Common in discussions, essays and interviews about ideas, character and social questions. The usual pattern is *A and B are two sides of the same coin*. Don't confuse it with *the other side of the coin*, which introduces the opposite aspect of a situation.
entries.pattern: A and B are two sides of the same coin
examples: For a lot of athletes, confidence and arrogance are **two sides of the same coin**.
The city's tourism boom and its housing shortage are **two sides of the same coin**.
In our family, my dad's stubbornness and his loyalty are really **two sides of the same coin**.

drill.sentence: Her perfectionism and her success are {{two sides of the same coin}}: the habit that wears her out is the one that got her promoted.
drill.hint: closely linked parts of one thing (a money image)

entries.related: *the other side of the coin* — the opposite aspect; *go hand in hand* — happen together; *a double-edged sword* — something with both good and bad effects.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say honestly and directly what you think, even if other people may not like it.
entries.usage: Usually positive, describing honesty or courage: *She's never afraid to speak her mind.* It often follows *afraid to*, *free to* or *not shy about*. The possessive matches the subject: *speak my / his / their mind*.
examples: Our neighbor Ruth has always **spoken her mind**, even at the fanciest dinner parties.
On this team, everyone is encouraged to **speak their mind** in meetings.
The new captain isn't afraid to **speak his mind**, even to the team's owner.

drill.sentence: My aunt always {{speaks her mind}}, so don't be surprised if she tells you your haircut is awful.
drill.hint: is completely open about her opinions (not *tells it like it is*)

entries.related: *speak up* — say something, especially to object; *tell it like it is* — describe things honestly, often bluntly; *bite your tongue* — the opposite, stop yourself from speaking.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make someone extremely angry, often because something seems unfair or cruel.
entries.usage: Informal and emotional; used about injustice, rudeness and cruelty. The most common frame is *It makes my blood boil when … / to see …*. It describes strong anger that builds inside, not necessarily shouting.
entries.pattern: It makes my blood boil when … / to see …
examples: It **makes my blood boil** when people throw trash out of their car windows.
Reading about the scam that targeted elderly people **made my blood boil**.
The way he talks to waiters really **makes my blood boil**.

drill.sentence: Seeing someone kick a dog {{makes my blood boil}}; I just can't stay calm.
drill.hint: fills me with rage (a hot-liquid image)

entries.related: *drive someone crazy* — annoy someone a lot; *get under someone's skin* — annoy someone in a lasting way; *see red* — suddenly become very angry.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Too proud of yourself and your abilities, in a way that seems arrogant and self-centered.
entries.usage: Informal and critical, usually after *be* or *seem*: *He's so full of himself.* The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject. Don't confuse it with *full of it*, which means talking nonsense or not telling the truth.
examples: Ever since he got promoted, Kevin's been really **full of himself**.
She's talented, but she's so **full of herself** that nobody wants to work with her.
I don't want to sound **full of myself**, but I make the best lasagna in the family.

drill.sentence: He spent the whole first date talking about his car and his workouts; he was so {{full of himself}}.
drill.hint: too pleased with his own importance (not *stuck-up* or *conceited*)

entries.related: *stuck-up* — acting superior to others; *conceited* — too proud, more formal; *have a big head* — think you are very important.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In good times and bad times; loyally, whatever difficulties come.
entries.usage: Warm and positive; used about loyalty in marriages, friendships, families and sports fans. It usually follows verbs like *stick with*, *stand by* or *be there for someone*. The form is fixed.
entries.pattern: stick with / stand by someone through thick and thin
examples: My college roommate has stuck with me **through thick and thin** for twenty years.
Cubs fans stayed loyal **through thick and thin**, waiting 108 years for a World Series title.
They've been married half a century and have supported each other **through thick and thin**.

drill.sentence: My parents ran their small grocery store together {{through thick and thin}}, including two recessions and a fire.
drill.hint: in good times and bad (not *for better or worse*)

entries.related: *for better or (for) worse* — whatever happens, from wedding vows; *come rain or shine* — whatever happens; *a fair-weather friend* — the opposite, a friend only in good times.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A large amount of money available to spend, especially for a person, company or organization.
entries.usage: Common in business, legal and sports news: *a team with deep pockets*. It often suggests power or an advantage, for example when people sue the party *with the deepest pockets*. The adjective is *deep-pocketed*: *a deep-pocketed investor*.
entries.pattern: have deep pockets; a company with deep pockets
examples: Only a buyer with **deep pockets** could afford a house in that neighborhood.
The Yankees have **deep pockets**, so they can outbid most teams for free agents.
Lawyers often go after the company with the **deepest pockets**, not the person most at fault.

drill.sentence: The little bookstore can't compete on price with an online giant that has such {{deep pockets}}.
drill.hint: lots of money to spend (a clothing image)

entries.related: *loaded* — very rich, informal; *cash-strapped* — the opposite, short of money; *money is no object* — the cost does not matter.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Old-fashioned; not aware of or not using modern ideas, methods or technology.
entries.usage: Often mildly critical, or self-mocking: *I know I'm behind the times, but I still use a paper calendar.* It is used about people, institutions and rules. Don't mix it up with *behind the curve*, which means reacting to a new development too late.
examples: I know I'm a little **behind the times**, but I still pay my rent with a paper check.
Our school district is way **behind the times**; kids still can't turn in homework online.
My seventy-year-old neighbor isn't as **behind the times** as you'd think; he has his own podcast.

drill.sentence: My parents are a bit {{behind the times}}; they still think you need a printed map for a road trip.
drill.hint: not up to date with modern life (not *out of touch*, *old-school* or *set in their ways*)

entries.related: *out of touch* — not aware of current events or feelings; *old school* — old-fashioned, often in a positive way; *ahead of your time* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A chance to live or work with new energy and happiness, for example after an illness or a hard period; also used about old things that become useful again.
entries.usage: Positive and common after *get*, *have* or *give*: *The surgery gave her a new lease on life.* It is used about people, pets, old buildings and products. British English says *a new lease of life*.
entries.pattern: get / give someone or something a new lease on life
examples: After his heart surgery, my uncle feels like he has **a new lease on life**.
My dad got **a new lease on life** when he started volunteering at the animal shelter after he retired.
A new coat of paint and a few repairs gave the old movie theater **a new lease on life**.

drill.sentence: The empty warehouse got {{a new lease on life}} when it was turned into a food hall.
drill.hint: a fresh start with new energy (a renting image; the American form)

entries.related: *a new lease of life* — the British form; *a fresh start* — a chance to begin again; *breathe new life into something* — make it active or interesting again.

entries.term: in a league of its own
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Much better than anything or anyone similar, so that a fair comparison is hardly possible.
entries.usage: Strongly positive, about people, places and products. The possessive changes: *in a league of her own*, *in a league of their own*. *In a class of its own* means the same.
entries.pattern: in a league of its / his / her / their own
examples: I've tried a lot of pizza in New York, but this place is **in a league of its own**.
As a pianist, she was **in a league of her own**; nobody else in the competition came close.
When it comes to customer service, that airline is **in a league of its own**.

drill.sentence: There are plenty of great hikes in Utah, but Angels Landing in Zion is {{in a league of its own}}.
drill.hint: far better than all similar ones (a sports image; not *in a class …*)

entries.related: *in a class of its own* — same; *second to none* — the best; *out of someone's league* — too good or attractive for someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop working properly and behave in a wild or uncontrolled way.
entries.usage: Informal and common about machines, electronics, systems and plans: *My phone went haywire after the update.* It suggests sudden, chaotic behavior rather than simply breaking down. It is mostly used about technology, sometimes about people's plans or emotions.
examples: The traffic lights downtown **went haywire** during the storm, and police had to direct cars.
My car's dashboard **went haywire** last night, and every warning light came on at once.
After the update, the app **went haywire** and sent everyone the same notification fifty times.

drill.sentence: During the heat wave, our thermostat {{went haywire}} and kept turning on the heat in the middle of the night.
drill.hint: started malfunctioning wildly (not *crazy* or *nuts*)

entries.related: *act up* — not work properly, milder; *on the fritz* — not working properly, informal American; *break down* — stop working completely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make people feel that something is wrong or dangerous and needs attention.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and everyday talk. The subject is the warning sign, and *for someone* can follow: *His answers set off alarm bells for the detectives.* *Ring alarm bells* is the same idiom and is more common in British English.
entries.pattern: something sets off alarm bells (for someone)
examples: A charge from a store in Brazil on my credit card **set off alarm bells**, since I've never been there.
His sudden weight loss **set off alarm bells** for his doctor.
The landlord's demand for cash only **set off alarm bells**, so we kept looking for an apartment.

drill.sentence: The email asked for my password and had three spelling mistakes, which immediately {{set off alarm bells}}.
drill.hint: made me suspect something was wrong (not *raised red flags*)

entries.related: *raise a red flag* — show that there may be a problem, very common in American English; *ring alarm bells* — same, more British; *smell a rat* — suspect a trick.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The people in a society or group who have money and resources, and the people who do not.
entries.usage: Used in news, economics and social commentary about inequality, often in *the gap between the haves and the have-nots*. Both *the haves and have-nots* and *the haves and the have-nots* are common. Note the hyphen in *have-nots*.
examples: The new airport lounges draw a clear line between **the haves and the have-nots** of air travel.
During the power outage, the street split into **the haves and the have-nots**: people with generators and people without.
In a city with sky-high rents, the gap between **the haves and have-nots** is visible on every block.

drill.sentence: At my high school, the line between {{the haves and the have-nots}} was obvious: some kids got new cars at sixteen, and others worked after school.
drill.hint: rich kids versus poor kids — two forms of one verb

entries.related: *the one percent* — the very richest people; *the less fortunate* — a polite term for poor people; *the well-off* — people with plenty of money.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To leave a difficult period behind and start a new, better one.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and speeches after a scandal, a loss, a divorce or a crisis. It is often said as a goal: *It's time to turn the page.* *Turn the page on* + the past period is also common, and the tone is hopeful.
entries.pattern: turn the page (on something)
examples: After the flood, the whole town was eager to rebuild Main Street and **turn the page**.
The divorce was painful, but she's ready to **turn the page** and start dating again.
The company apologized for the data leak and said it was time to **turn the page**.

drill.sentence: After two years of rehab and a lot of hard work, Josh finally feels ready to {{turn the page}} on that part of his life.
drill.hint: leave the past behind (a book image; not *move on* or *close the book*)

entries.related: *move on* — stop thinking about the past; *close the book on something* — end it completely; *turn over a new leaf* — change your own behavior for the better.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Whatever the weather is, or whatever happens; in all conditions.
entries.usage: Common in event announcements and everyday talk: *The market is open rain or shine.* It usually comes at the end of a clause, sometimes at the start. *Come rain or shine* means the same and sounds a little more emphatic.
examples: The farmers market is open every Saturday morning, **rain or shine**.
My neighbor walks his dog at six every morning, **rain or shine**.
**Rain or shine**, our mail carrier shows up at the door by noon.

drill.sentence: Our kids' soccer games are played {{rain or shine}}, so pack a raincoat and an extra pair of socks.
drill.hint: no matter what the weather is like (not *no matter what*)

entries.related: *come rain or shine* — same, more emphatic; *come what may* — whatever happens, more formal; *no matter what* — plainer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In writing, so that it is clear and official; also, seen in simple terms of right and wrong, with no middle ground.
entries.usage: In the first sense it often follows *see it*, *put it* or *get it*: *I want it in black and white.* In the second sense it criticizes oversimplified thinking: *She sees everything in black and white.* Before a noun it becomes *black-and-white*: *a black-and-white issue*.
examples: The rules are right there **in black and white**: no pets in the building.
I won't believe I got the raise until I see it **in black and white**.
Teenagers often see the world **in black and white**, but life isn't that simple.

drill.sentence: Before we paid the deposit, we asked the wedding venue to put its refund policy {{in black and white}}.
drill.hint: written down clearly (a color image; not *in writing*)

entries.related: *in writing* — plain and neutral; *spelled out* — explained in detail; *shades of gray* — the opposite of black-and-white thinking.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To manage to say something when another person is talking so much that there is hardly any chance to speak.
entries.usage: Informal and almost always negative: *I couldn't get a word in edgewise.* It is a complaint, often humorous, about someone who talks nonstop. British English says *edgeways*.
examples: My aunt talked for an hour straight; nobody could **get a word in edgewise**.
The two hosts kept interrupting each other, and the guest never **got a word in edgewise**.
Once my kids start telling stories about school, I can't **get a word in edgewise**.

drill.sentence: The salesman talked so fast about the car's features that I couldn't {{get a word in edgewise}} to ask about the price.
drill.hint: manage to say anything at all (the American form)

entries.related: *get a word in edgeways* — the British form; *talk someone's ear off* — talk to someone for too long; *cut someone off* — interrupt them.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A tight feeling in the throat that you get when you are moved and close to crying.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about emotional moments: weddings, goodbyes, speeches and films. The usual patterns are *have / get a lump in your throat* and *bring a lump to your throat*. It can come from sadness, pride or love.
entries.pattern: have / get a lump in your throat; bring a lump to someone's throat
examples: I had **a lump in my throat** when my daughter walked across the stage at graduation.
Hearing my grandfather's voice on an old voicemail gave me **a lump in my throat**.
The best man had **a lump in his throat** as he raised his glass to the couple.

drill.sentence: When the soldier surprised his little sister at school, everyone in the gym had {{a lump in their throat}}.
drill.hint: a tight feeling from holding back tears (not *tears in their eyes*)

entries.related: *choke up* — become unable to speak because of emotion; *tear up* — start to have tears in your eyes; *moved to tears* — so touched that you cry.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stay out of other people's private affairs; as a command, a firm or rude way to say that something is not someone's concern.
entries.usage: As a command, *Mind your own business!* is rude and angry. In stories, *minding my own business* is neutral and shows you did nothing to cause what happened: *I was just minding my own business when …* To refuse to answer a personal question, people also say *None of your business.*
examples: When my neighbor asked how much we paid for the house, I wanted to tell him to **mind his own business**.
I was just sitting on the bus, **minding my own business**, when a man started yelling at me.
In a small town, it's hard to **mind your own business**; everyone knows everything.

drill.sentence: My nosy coworker keeps asking about my salary. I wish she'd just {{mind her own business}}.
drill.hint: stay out of other people's affairs (not *butt out*)

entries.related: *none of your business* — said to refuse a personal question; *butt out* — stop interfering, rude and informal; *nosy* — too interested in other people's lives.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To refuse to help or support someone who needs you or who expected your loyalty.
entries.usage: Often emotional and critical: *He turned his back on his own family.* It can also be used about ideas, places and careers: *turn your back on medicine*. In the negative it promises loyalty: *I'll never turn my back on you.*
entries.pattern: turn your back on someone / something
examples: When he lost everything, most of his so-called friends **turned their backs on him**.
Whatever happens, I'll never **turn my back on** my little brother.
After the fire, the town didn't **turn its back on** the Garcias; neighbors raised enough money to rebuild their home.

drill.sentence: Her parents {{turned their backs on her}} when she dropped out of law school, but her aunt let her stay for a year.
drill.hint: refused to support her — a body image (not *cut her off*)

entries.related: *abandon* — leave someone completely, more formal; *cut someone off* — stop giving someone money or contact; *stand by someone* — the opposite, stay loyal.

entries.term: there's no such thing as a free lunch
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: You cannot get something for nothing; anything that seems free has a hidden cost.
entries.usage: A common saying, used as a warning in conversation, economics and business, often about offers that look too good to be true. It is a fixed full sentence. People sometimes shorten it: *There's no free lunch.*
examples: The app is free, but it sells your data. **There's no such thing as a free lunch**.
The free vacation came with a three-hour timeshare presentation; **there's no such thing as a free lunch**.
My dad taught me early that **there's no such thing as a free lunch**: if someone offers you something for nothing, ask what they want.

drill.sentence: The gym offered me a month at no charge, but only if I signed a one-year contract. {{There's no such thing as a free lunch}}.
drill.hint: nothing comes without a cost (a meal image)

entries.related: *too good to be true* — so good that it is probably a trick; *you get what you pay for* — cheap things are low quality; *there's a catch* — there is a hidden problem.
entries.origin: From 19th-century American bars that offered a free lunch to customers, who paid for it by buying drinks.
